# Arbitrary convex fibers: boundary variances and corrected mixed flux

This note extends the variance and flux interface to arbitrary positive full-dimensional convex fibers. It uses no polyhedral approximation and makes no polyhedral-attainment assumption. It also corrects the sign of the cap covariance in the integer-coordinate flux identity in the earlier `candidate 22fb802a1dc82eb3`.

The extension remains a necessary-condition theorem. Its variance terms have no asserted common sign after multiplication by their different normals, and it does not prove OC. The measure throughout is ordinary positive `d`-volume on each fiber, with `d>=1`. An intrinsic intersection of dimension less than `d` is not implicitly covered.

## 1. Actual data, measures, and the boundary coupling

Let `P` be a finite subset of `R^n`, let each `K_p` be a compact convex body in `R^d`, and assume these are the actual sections at `p` of

    C=conv union_(p in P) ({p} times K_p).

No lattice change or integration over the base is used. In the intended mixed-integer application `P` is the actual finite integer base. Write `mu` for the sum of the fiber `d`-volume measures, and write `eta` for the sum of the fiber boundary `H_(d-1)` measures, marked with the unique outer unit continuous normal at almost every boundary point. For `d=1`, each interval has two endpoints with `H_0` mass one and normals `-1,+1`.

These boundary measures are finite. For example, coordinate graph integration gives

    integral_(boundary K) |n_l| dH_(d-1)
       =2 |projection_(e_l perp) K|,

and `sum_l |n_l|>=1`. A finite enclosing box bounds the right sides. The normal is Borel on its full-measure regular set, as follows from the local convex graph charts.

Assume `nu=f eta` is finite and nonnegative and that its physical marginal is in equal-mass convex order below that of `eta`. The fully proved compact transport theorem in `candidate 7278f286325c46c7` supplies a coupling `Pi` from `nu` to `eta` with conditional physical output mean equal to its input. Since the fibers are actual, the same source proves that the continuous normal is preserved. Equivalently, for all bounded Borel source tests `h`,

    integral h(u,w)(w'-w) dPi=0,
    u'=u almost everywhere.                          (1)

This is the only transport existence dependency. No new transport theorem or regularity of the convex bodies is presumed below.

## 2. Bounded Borel labels by actual support planes

Let `E=aff P`, of dimension `r`. For each unit continuous normal `u`, set `h_p(u)=max_(x in K_p) u.x`. The actual-fiber assumption gives

    h_p(u)=max{sum_q alpha_q h_q(u):
                alpha>=0, sum alpha=1, sum alpha_q q=p}.         (2)

The inequality from right to left follows by taking actual maximizing points in each fiber and their convex combination; the single-base representation gives equality.

Finite linear-programming duality for (2), or equivalently the upper faces of the convex hull of `(q,h_q(u))`, gives an affine majorant `l` of all the heights that touches at `p`. It can be chosen among the interpolants through `r+1` affinely independent bases. Here are the finite-basis details: the dual polyhedron is nonempty; its recession lineality is zero because `P` affinely spans `E`; its nonempty optimal face therefore has a vertex. At a vertex the active evaluation functionals span the `r+1`-dimensional affine-function space. Choosing a basis of active evaluations gives precisely such an interpolant. In dimension zero the sole interpolant is the constant height.

List these finitely many interpolants as

    l_j(u,z)=b_j(u)-a_j(u).z.

Their coefficients are continuous and uniformly bounded in `u`: each is a fixed linear function of finitely many continuous bounded support functions. If `E` is a proper affine subspace, choose its linear coefficients in its direction space and extend by zero on its orthogonal complement. This is an extension of a real affine functional, not a transformation of the lattice.

At a regular marked point `(u,p,x)`, choose the first interpolant that majorizes all heights and touches at `p`. The choice is Borel, because it involves finitely many continuous inequalities and equalities. Denote its label by

    theta=(j,u),
    a(theta)=a_j(u), b(theta)=b_j(u), u(theta)=u.

The associated actual exposed face is

    F_theta=C intersect {a(theta).z+u(theta).x=b(theta)}.         (3)

It need not be a facet and may have any affine dimension. Every source lies on its selected face. Every output in that source row stays on the same face: the supporting-plane gap is nonnegative, bounded, and has conditional mean zero by (1). This argument uses Borel bounded coefficient tests, so it does not require intersecting uncountably many probability-one events.

## 3. Disintegrated variance on the actual faces

Lift `Pi` by the source label `theta`, and let `kappa` be its label marginal. The label space is a finite set times the compact sphere. Disintegrate this finite Borel measure with respect to `kappa`, writing its conditional probability as `Pi_theta` and its two physical marginals as `nu_theta,eta_theta`. A zero-total-mass case is omitted. For `kappa`-almost every label,

    integral (1,w) d(eta_theta-nu_theta)=0,
    supp Pi_theta subset F_theta times F_theta.                 (4)

Normal preservation is also retained. These assertions follow by localizing (1) with every bounded label test; a finite list of coordinate identities suffices to choose a simultaneous null set.

Put `W_theta=eta_theta-nu_theta` and `delta=w'-w`. The actual variance matrix is

    Q_theta=integral w w^T dW_theta
           =integral delta delta^T dPi_theta >=0.                (5)

Indeed, the two cross terms in the quadratic expansion vanish by the row barycenter identity. All integrands are bounded on a fixed compact set. Since every increment is tangent to the plane (3),

    Q_theta (a(theta),u(theta))=0.                               (6)

These are Borel, integrably bounded matrix fields. Alternatively, (5) defines a finite positive-semidefinite matrix-valued measure in `theta`; disintegration is merely a convenient notation.

Write `B_theta=Q_theta^(px)`. The block identities are

    Q_theta^(pp) a(theta)+B_theta u(theta)=0,
    B_theta^T a(theta)+Q_theta^(xx) u(theta)=0.                    (7)

These formulas replace the finite facet sums by integrals over actual support-plane labels. They do not replace an actual face by a tangent approximation.

The target ownership is transport-induced. More precisely, the lifted target law disintegrates as `eta(dw) Omega_w(dtheta)`, where `Omega_w` is a probability kernel. The source uses its deterministic label `sigma(w)`. Thus the labeled signed difference is

    eta(dw) Omega_w(dtheta)-nu(dw) delta_(sigma(w))(dtheta).      (8)

There is no assertion that target and source ownership agree. Positive boundary mass at a shared face is retained in these kernels.

## 4. Fiber Gauss–Green, with every supporting-cap status

For completeness the only boundary integration identity needed here can be obtained without approximating a convex body. For a fixed coordinate direction, almost every parallel line meets a convex body in an interval `[alpha(y),beta(y)]`. Fubini and the one-dimensional fundamental theorem give

    integral_K partial_l V_l
       =integral [V_l(y,beta(y))-V_l(y,alpha(y))] dy.

The upper and lower endpoint graphs are locally Lipschitz over the projection interior. Their graph area formula identifies the right side with `integral_(boundary K) V_l n_l`; the remaining boundary has zero weighted measure for `|n_l|`. Summing the coordinates gives Gauss–Green for the polynomial fields used below. In dimension one it is the fundamental theorem itself. The same argument applies to any proper positive-volume cap, which is again a convex body. No limiting sequence of bodies appears.

Fix a nonvertical closed cap

    H_j={a_j.p+v_j.x>=b_j},       |v_j|=1.

On strict body traces let `alpha_j` be its indicator. On an inside supporting coincidence use `alpha_j+sigma_j=1`, with both in `[0,1]`; on an outside supporting coincidence use `alpha_j=sigma_j`. Define `zeta_j` on the cap plane by full section area on proper cuts and by `sigma_j` times the supporting face area on supporting cuts. Empty/full cuts away from the boundary contribute no section measure. This is exactly the consistent allocation convention of the original stress theorem.

For every polynomial vector field `V(x)`, the fiber-summed flux identity is

    integral_(H_j) div V dmu
       =integral alpha_j V.n deta
                    -integral V.v_j dzeta_j.                   (9)

On a proper cut the new cap boundary has outward normal `-v_j`, proving the sign. At an inside supporting face the body normal is `-v_j`; its right-hand contribution is `-(alpha_j+sigma_j)V.v_j`, the full-body contribution. At an outside supporting face its normal is `v_j`; the right-hand contribution is `(alpha_j-sigma_j)V.v_j=0`, as the captured `d`-volume is zero. Thus (9) includes positive supporting-face mass, both extreme allocations, and all zero-area supporting faces. It includes `d=1` with counting section measure. The sections and their moments are finite because there are finitely many bounded convex fibers.

## 5. Corrected arbitrary-body moment identities

Assume now

    f=sum_j lambda_j alpha_j,       lambda_j>=0,

with finitely many caps and the matching boundary coupling above. Group the positive-section caps into circuits `i`. Assume the following actual section-stress identities, exactly as in the prior polytopal theorem:

    S_j=zeta_j(total)>0,
    lambda_j S_j=t_i rho_j,
    centroid(zeta_j)=wbar_i=(pbar_i,xbar_i),
    sum_(j in i) rho_j(b_j-a_j.pbar_i)=0.                      (10)

Zero-weight caps may be dropped. A zero section measure contributes no moments; the displayed centroid hypothesis is only made for nonzero measures. These conditions are explicit inputs, not inferred anew from arbitrary selected caps.

Let

    V_j=integral (w-wbar_i)(w-wbar_i)^T dzeta_j.

Then `V_j>=0` and `V_j(a_j,v_j)=0`, because the actual section is in its cap plane. Define full mixed moments `m_p=integral p dmu`, `m_x=integral x dmu` and the corresponding cap moments `m_pj,m_xj`. The exact identities are

    d(m_p-sum_j lambda_j m_pj)
      =-integral Q_theta^(pp) a(theta) dkappa(theta)
                    -sum_j lambda_j V_j^(pp) a_j,              (11)

    (d+1)(m_x-sum_j lambda_j m_xj)
      = integral Q_theta^(xx) u(theta) dkappa(theta)
                    +sum_j lambda_j V_j^(xx) v_j.              (12)

**Both terms on the right of (11) have minus signs.**

To prove (11), apply (9) to `V(x)=x`, multiply by the fixed base `p`, and subtract the weighted cap identities from the full-body identity. The raw formula is

    d(m_p-sum lambda_j m_pj)
       =integral p(n.x) d(eta-nu)
                       +sum_j lambda_j integral p(b_j-a_j.p) dzeta_j.

The raw section sign is plus because the cap identity (9) already has a minus. Disintegrating the first term by the actual labels gives `-integral Q_theta^(pp)a(theta) dkappa`, using (3)–(5). Expanding each section term at its centroid gives

    S_j pbar_i(b_j-a_j.pbar_i)-V_j^(pp)a_j.

The first terms cancel by (10). This proves (11).

For (12), test `V(x)=x(h.x)`, whose divergence is `(d+1)h.x`, for each constant `h`. The same subtraction and centroid cancellation give

    (d+1)(m_x-sum lambda_j m_xj)
       =-integral B_theta^T a(theta) dkappa
                       -sum_j lambda_j C_j^T a_j,

where `C_j=V_j^(px)`. Applying (7) and the cap covariance kernel converts these two terms into (12). Every integral is finite, since the support-plane coefficients and the covariance matrices are bounded and `kappa` is finite.

The cap allocations are unchanged by the support-plane disintegration: each `alpha_j eta` is placed on the same deterministic source label, whereas the target uses (8). In particular, this proof neither substitutes a full tangent section for an allocated one nor reassigns cap branches to fit the transport.

## 6. Exact genuine-critical certificate for the sign correction

Take `n=d=1`, `P={-1,0,1}`, and `K_p=[-1/2,1/2]`. The actual body is the rectangle `[-1,1] times [-1/2,1/2]`, with mixed mass three. At `Y=(0,0)`, every nonvertical through-center cap has mass `3/2` by symmetry and zero boundary mass; every pure-integer containing cap has mass at least two. Thus the raw global depth is `Q=3/2`: every candidate point has a nonvertical containing halfspace of mass at most half the total.

Consider the genuine critical caps

    H1={x+p/4>=0},       H2={-x>=0}.

Use `lambda_1=lambda_2=rho_1=rho_2=1`. Their section masses are three, their section centroids are both `(0,0)`, and (10) holds with `t_i=3`. Their strict body boundary traces sum to one, so `nu=eta`; the identity coupling has every `Q_theta=0`.

Direct interval integration gives

    m_p=0,       m_p1=1/2,       m_p2=0,
    V_1^(pp)=V_2^(pp)=2,
    a_1=1/4,     a_2=0.

Thus (11) reads `-1/2=-1/2`. The formerly printed plus sign in front of the cap covariance would assert `-1/2=+1/2`. This countercheck satisfies the complete stated section-stress and martingale hypotheses, not merely an arbitrary algebraic matrix choice.

For an independent check of (12),

    m_x=0, m_x1=5/16, m_x2=-3/8,
    V_1^(xx)=1/8, V_2^(xx)=0,

so both sides of (12) equal `1/8`.

## 7. Exact scope of the extension

The finite facet partition was a convenience, not a necessary geometric hypothesis: a bounded Borel support-plane selector and its transport-induced target kernels replace it completely. Fiberwise Gauss–Green requires only positive full-dimensional convex fibers. All covariance, kernel, and moment identities therefore apply to an arbitrary convex-body attained minimum whenever its already proved boundary stress and the explicit section identities (10) are available.

The remaining limitation is numerical, not a missing passage from polytopes. Positive-semidefinite matrices multiplied by different mixed normals need not point in a common direction, and neither integral in (11) nor (12) is assigned a useful sign by this theorem. The existing actual nonzero-variance example remains valid. No sharp depth estimate follows from the extension alone.

## 8. A curved actual family with nonzero support-face covariance

The integral labeling is necessary even for a simple smooth-fiber example. Take `n=1,d=2`, a nonzero vector `t in R^2`, and

    P={-1,0,1},      K_p=p t+r B_2,       r>0.

Their actual convex hull is the sheared circular cylinder

    {-1<=z<=1, x-z t in r B_2}.

At each unit normal `u`, the three measured boundary points are `(p,p t+r u)`. Give the central boundary circle source density three and the other two circles source density zero; the target has density one on each. Send each central source row equally to the three corresponding points. This is an actual physical martingale preserving the continuous normal.

The chosen support plane has `a(u)=-u.t`, `b(u)=r`. With angular parameter `theta`, its label mass is `dkappa=3r dtheta`. Its conditional covariance is

    Q_u=(2/3) (1,t)(1,t)^T,
    Q_u(-u.t,u)=0.

For almost every angle the ambient support face is only a line segment, not an ambient facet. Nevertheless the covariance is nonzero, and all formulas in Sections 2–3 apply. Thus strict convexity of the individual fibers does not make this transport deterministic or remove the mixed covariance. This is a transport calibration, not an asserted critical-cap stress or a depth counterexample.
